log.a:
No. Let L be the losing hat configurations. Any winning configuration must differ in one bit from some configuration in L: flip a player who makes a correct guess, making that same guess wrong. Thus L is a dominating set of the 100-cube.

The standard excess bound for hypercube domination says γ(Q_n) ≥ 2^n/n when n is not of the form 2^m−1. Hence |L| ≥ 2^100/100, so success probability is at most 1−1/100=99%. Therefore it cannot exceed 99% (though it may attain 99% only if an optimal dominating set exists).
log.b:
Pair each element g with its inverse g⁻¹. Elements not equal to their inverses form disjoint two-element pairs. Since |G| is even, the number of self-inverse elements must also be even. The identity is one, so there must be another, x ≠ e. Then x² = e, hence x has order 2.

Finiteness is used in the parity count: removing two-element pairs from a finite even-sized set leaves an even-sized set. This inference fails for infinite sets; for example, the infinite group (ℤ, +) has no element of order 2.
